newsitem.title: PERU: Peru unflinching on rebel demands in hostage siege.
newsitem.headline: Peru unflinching on rebel demands in hostage siege.

text.p: Peru refused to bow on Friday to Marxist hostage-takers' demands but said it still hoped for a peaceful solution to the plight of nearly 400 ailing captives held for three days in the Japanese embassy residence.

Reflecting growing desperation inside the building, hostages thrust up signs in various languages from a second floor window on Friday pleading for water, electricity and telephones to be reconnected and food to be brought.
There was no immediate response from authorities to the crudely lettered pleas in Japanese, German, English and Spanish.

"The situation inside is difficult. There is overcrowding, it is very hot," Red Cross official Sergio Natarajan said after visiting the residence. "Among the illnesses are diabetes, ulcers, heart problems and diarrhoea."

Outside the besieged residence, anguished relatives trying to bring food, medicines and clothing to their loved ones jostled with police calling for order. Family members clutching candles had prayed through the night for the victim's lives.

Adding to the tension, a caller claiming to be from the MRTA phoned Lima's CPN radio station to warn authorities against any commando attack on the residence and to denounce President Alberto Fujimori as a "coward".
"We don't want any attack or any assault," the unidentified caller said. "We know we're dead anyway and there's nothing left but for us all to die together."
Fujimori has kept a stony public silence since the crisis broke on Tuesday, closeting himself with generals in a barracks and ignoring all the known rebel demands.

But his prime minister Alberto Pandolfi said on Friday international condemnation of the guerrillas and support for the government "gives us the peace and strength of mind to trust that we will reach a peaceful solution".
Overnight, the government refused point blank the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) main demand: the release of jailed comrades, including their leader Victor Polay.
Intelligence officers even visited Polay and other imprisoned MRTA leaders to try to persuade them -- so far without success -- to publicly condemn the siege, police sources said.

Around 20 MRTA rebels stormed the residence in a commando- style assault on Tuesday night to protest against free-market economic policies and show the world that Marxist guerrillas were still a force to be reckoned with in Peru.

Red Cross workers ferried in containers of water, soft drinks, salads, cake and medicines to the portals of the elegant residence on Friday morning but there was no visible progress in negotiations and no mediators were seen entering.

There was one brief ray of hope when hostages raised a sign on Friday morning in Japanese which seemed to indicate more hostages could be released. It read, "OK to leave again" and underneath in smaller characters "All hostages".
But by mid-afternoon, no more captives had been set free.
Red Cross officials are the official negotiators between the government and the rebels holding the array of ministers, ambassadors and businessmen. Peru's anti-terrorism chief is among the captives.
As rumours swirled of possible military solutions, Japan signalled it was not happy with Fujimori's hardline stance.
Worried about the safety of dozens of Japanese held inside the residence, Tokyo said it was "far apart in ideas" over how to solve the crisis. It did not go into details.

Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived on Thursday to help with negotiations, talked to Red Cross, U.S. and Canadian mediators on Friday to try to find a way out of the plight but had no immediate plans to see Fujimori again following a brief first meeting on Thursday night.
Like other countries with nationals held inside the residence, Tokyo said saving the lives of the hostages should be the top priority.

Police sources said all options were under review for ending the siege, including a lightning military assault but there was no official word on the matter. Britain and the United States have sent in expert teams to advise Peru.
As the embassy residence is considered Japanese territory, international law requires Fujimori to seek Tokyo's approval for any attack.

So far, Fujimori's hard line with the guerrillas is playing well to local public opinion. Peruvians say they do not want to see the government cave in to the guerrillas' demands for the release of jailed comrades.

Fujimori ignored an ultimatum by the rebels to come and talk in person on Wednesday. In a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton sent on Thursday he said the safety of hostages would be his top priority.
Attempts by the MRTA and the previously better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
